lessonTitle: Stages of the Design Process: From Need to Tested Prototype

blocks.text: A team spends ten weeks machining a shopping trolley that climbs stairs, then learns on test day that the client's building has spiral staircases the trolley cannot turn on. A single ten-minute question in week one would have caught it. The design process exists to find such mistakes while they are cheap.

blocks.markdown: The design process turns a client's need into a tested product through a sequence of stages. Each stage has a purpose and an **output**, a document or artefact that the next stage uses. Skipping an output, such as the specification, means the next stage works from guesses.

rows: What problem does the client have?
Need statement, user and context notes
How will we know a solution is good enough?
Numbered, measurable requirements with test methods
What different ways could we solve it?
Several concepts, one selected with reasons
Drawings, tolerances, bill of materials, manufacturing plan
Test results compared with each requirement
blocks.caption: Stages of a simple linear design process.

blocks.title: Need statement versus specification
blocks.text: A **need statement** describes the problem or the user's goal, in solution-neutral words, for example: 'Residents need to carry shopping up stairs without lifting it.' A **design specification** lists measurable requirements each with a target value and a test, for example: 'Carry a 20 kg load up 15 steps of 180 mm rise; device mass at most 8 kg.' The need says why, the specification says how well.

blocks.markdown: A need statement must not contain a solution (a trolley with wheels) or it closes off alternatives. A specification must not be vague (easy to use, strong) or it cannot be verified. The first is a statement of purpose; the second is a set of tests the finished design will be judged against.

blocks.title: Converting a need into specification items
blocks.prompt: Need: 'Cyclists need a way to secure a bike outside a shop for an hour.' Write three specification items.

steps.text: Identify the aspects of the need that can be measured: the time the bike must be secured, the resistance to attack, and the size of bike it must work with.

Give each aspect a target value and a test: 'Resist hand-tool attack for at least 3 min (timed test with a 300 mm bolt cutter)'; 'Fit frame tubes 25 to 60 mm in diameter (gauge check)'; 'Mass at most 1.5 kg (weighing)'.
Check that none of the items names a solution such as a D-lock; each describes a performance or constraint that several solutions could satisfy.

blocks.answer: The statement says why, and three numbered requirements with targets and tests say how well.

blocks.markdown: **Iteration.** Real projects loop back. A prototype may reveal that a requirement was wrong, or a concept may turn out too costly to detail. The cost of fixing an error rises sharply with each stage, because more work has been built on the mistake, so finding errors early with cheap models, calculations and client reviews reduces risk.

blocks.caption: Probability that an error is still undetected after n independent reviews, each of which detects a fraction d of the errors present.

blocks.title: Iteration reduces risk: expected cost and review survival
blocks.prompt: (a) An error in a requirement has probability 30 % of being present. Fixing it at the specification review costs 1 unit; discovered at final testing it costs 60 units. Compare the expected cost. (b) Two reviews each detect 60 % of remaining errors: what fraction survives both?

steps.text: Expected cost = probability x cost. At the specification review: 0.30 x 1 = 0.3 units.
At final testing: 0.30 x 60 = 18 units, so late discovery costs 17.7 units more on average.
For two reviews with d = 0.6, an error survives each review with probability 0.4.
Evaluate: 0.4 x 0.4 = 0.16, so 16 % of errors survive two reviews.

blocks.answer: Early checking cuts the expected cost from 18 to 0.3 units; two reviews let through 16 % of errors.

items: Need: describe the problem, not the product.
Specification: every line has a target value and a test.
Concept: generate at least three options and select with stated criteria.
Detail: produce the drawings and plan that a workshop can build from.
Test: compare results to each requirement and record pass or fail.

blocks.title: Iteration is planned, not a failure
blocks.text: Going back is normal and expected. A loop from concept back to specification after a client review is cheap; the same discovery after manufacture is expensive. Plan early, cheap tests (sketches, cardboard mock-ups, calculations) to expose wrong assumptions.

blocks.title: The specification is not a wish list
blocks.text: If a requirement cannot be tested it cannot be used to decide whether the design succeeded. Words like 'robust', 'user-friendly' and 'lightweight' must be turned into numbers before the concept stage begins.

points: The process runs need, specification, concept, detail design and prototype/test, each stage producing an output that the next uses.
A need statement is a solution-neutral description of the problem; a specification is a set of measurable requirements with targets and test methods.
Iteration finds errors while changes are cheap; expected cost is probability times cost, and repeated reviews reduce the fraction of errors that survive.

questions.stem: Which stage of the design process produces the selected concept together with the reasons for choosing it?

distractorRationale.b: The need stage describes the problem, not the solutions.
distractorRationale.c: Detail design takes a chosen concept and produces drawings and tolerances.
distractorRationale.d: Testing verifies a built prototype against the specification.

questions.explanation: The concept stage is where alternatives are generated and compared and one is chosen, with documented criteria. Detail design only starts once a concept has been selected.

questions.stem: A project has finished drawings, tolerances, a bill of materials and a manufacturing plan. Which stage has just been completed?

distractorRationale.b: The specification is a set of requirements, not drawings.
distractorRationale.c: Concept generation produces sketches and principles rather than tolerances.
distractorRationale.d: The need stage gives a problem description.

questions.explanation: Drawings, tolerances, bill of materials and manufacturing plan are the outputs of detail design, which turns the chosen concept into something that a workshop can make. A specification or a concept sketch would not contain this level of manufacturing detail.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a need statement?

options.text: Hospital porters need a way to move heavy linen carts between floors without strain
A cart with four 150 mm castors and a 600 mm handle height
The cart must carry 120 kg and mass at most 25 kg
The handle shall be tested with a 400 N pull

questions.correctOptionText: Hospital porters need a way to move heavy linen carts between floors without strain

distractorRationale.b: This names a particular solution, with dimensions.
distractorRationale.c: This is a performance requirement with target values, so it belongs in a specification.
distractorRationale.d: This is a test method with a value, part of a specification.

questions.explanation: A need statement describes the user's problem and does not contain a solution or measurable targets. The other items name hardware or carry numbers, so they belong to later stages.

questions.stem: A team builds a cardboard mock-up in the concept stage and finds the handle is too short for taller users. What best explains why this reduces project risk?

options.text: The error is found when changing it costs almost nothing, instead of after parts have been made
Mock-ups remove the need to write a specification
Cardboard tests verify the final strength requirement
Iteration shows that the process has failed and should restart from the need

questions.correctOptionText: The error is found when changing it costs almost nothing, instead of after parts have been made

distractorRationale.b: The specification is still needed; the mock-up checks an assumption.
distractorRationale.d: Iteration is a normal part of the process and does not mean failure.

questions.explanation: The cost of correcting an error grows with the work built upon it. A cheap model reveals the wrong dimension before tooling or machining exists.

questions.stem: Returning from prototype testing to the concept stage means the design process has failed and should be avoided.
questions.explanation: Iteration is an expected part of the process and loops back whenever evidence contradicts an assumption. The aim is to arrange for these loops to occur early using cheap tests, so that fewer expensive loops occur late.

questions.stem: A requirement error has a probability of 25 % of being present. Fixing it at concept stage would cost 3 units, but if found at final testing it costs 120 units. What is the expected extra cost, in units, of finding it at testing rather than at concept stage?
questions.explanation: The expected extra cost is the probability times the extra cost: $0.25\times(120-3)=29.25$ units. This shows why early review is worthwhile even if the error is only a possibility.

questions.stem: A design review team detects 55 % of the errors present at each of three independent reviews. What percentage of the original errors survive all three reviews?
questions.explanation: Each review lets through $1-0.55=0.45$ of the errors, so after three reviews $0.45^3=0.0911$, or 9.11 %. More reviews reduce the survivors geometrically.

questions.stem: A client says: 'We need a better way to carry a wheelchair's folded ramp on the back of a bus.' (a) State whether this is a need statement or a specification and why, and (b) write three specification items, each with a target and test method.
markingGuide: Identifies that it is a need statement: describes the problem without a solution or measurable targets
Three specification lines each with a numeric target, for example mass, stowed length or load capacity
Each line has a test method such as weighing, measuring or load test
Lines are consistent with the stated need
questions.explanation: A need statement describes the purpose of the product and a specification gives measurable targets and tests. Each of the three items must have both a value and a way of checking it.

questions.stem: List the stages of the design process in order and state the output of each stage for the design of a wall-mounted bicycle rack.
markingGuide: Need: need statement (for example cyclists need to store bikes securely off the floor)
Specification: measurable requirements with test methods
Concept: several concepts and the selected one with reasons
Detail design: drawings, tolerances, bill of materials, manufacturing plan
Prototype and test: test results compared with the specification
questions.explanation: The stages run need, specification, concept, detail and test. A full answer links an output to each stage and uses the bicycle rack as the example rather than naming generic documents.

questions.stem: Explain, using an example, how iteration between stages reduces the risk of a failed design. Refer to the cost of changes at different stages.
markingGuide: Cost of changing a design rises as more work depends on the earlier decision
Early cheap tests (calculation, mock-up, client review) expose wrong assumptions
Concrete example of a loop, such as testing a model to find a dimension error before manufacturing
Loops from test back to specification or concept are expected
Repeated reviews reduce the chance that an error survives to the end
questions.explanation: Iteration lets the team check assumptions while a change is still cheap, so fewer large errors survive to prototype or production. A good example describes a specific early check and the late cost it avoids.
